name: cmd-stream (with MUS codec)
workload: Echo-style Distributed-Command-Pattern RPC over TCP with 30ms simulated server processing delay, payloads 17-1024 bytes, 1/2/4/8/16 concurrent client goroutines (go test -bench BenchmarkQPS).
claimed_speedup: ~3.15x more QPS than grpc-go/Protobuf at 1 client (145,352 vs 46,142 QPS) rising to ~4.56x at 16 clients (288,727 vs 63,285 QPS) (derived from page data: results/qps/qps.csv)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U with Radeon Graphics, Debian 6.1.148-1 x86_64 (single laptop, charger connected, fan at full speed)
tradeoffs: Custom Distributed Command Pattern rather than classic request/response RPC; peak speedup requires the companion MUS binary codec (codec-mus-stream-go), which needs code generation; JSON codec variant is much closer to gRPC in throughput.
caveats: Benchmark repo (go-client-server-benchmarks) is maintained by the same author as cmd-stream, so not an independent third party, though methodology/hardware/compiler are fully disclosed (kept at tier A per hard rules: 'who ran it does not matter'). Single-laptop run, not a controlled datacenter environment; no repeated-run variance reported beyond -count=10.
found_via: Hacker News (hn.algolia.com) search 'faster than gRPC' -> Show HN: Go Command-streaming lib for distributed systems (3x faster than gRPC)

name: Kitex
workload: Echo RPC service, Kitex's gRPC-compatible transport vs official grpc-go, 1KB request/response, concurrency swept 100-1000, client pinned to 16 CPUs / server to 4 CPUs.
claimed_speedup: ~1.7x higher QPS than grpc-go at concurrency=1000 (~195,000 QPS for Kitex vs ~114,000 QPS for gRPC) (derived from page data: docs/images/grpc_qps.png chart, values read off the chart, approximate)
hardware: Client pinned to 16 CPU cores, server pinned to 4 CPU cores (exact CPU model, OS, and Go version not stated in README or linked blog post)
stars_or_usage: 8052 stars; used in production at ByteDance
tradeoffs: Kitex is primarily a Thrift-first framework (gRPC support is one of several transport/codec combinations); its own docs caution 'performance benchmark can only provide a limited reference' since production factors vary.
caveats: Numbers were read off a chart image (docs/images/grpc_qps.png) rather than a tabulated CSV; CPU model, OS, and Go/compiler version are not stated, so this is the project's own benchmark with partial methodology, capped at tier C per the rules.
found_via: gh api repos/cloudwego/kitex + repos/cloudwego/kitex-benchmark (found after cross-checking Kitex, mentioned in cmd-stream's own comparison benchmark suite)

name: rpcx
baseline: gRPC (grpc-go); also compared against Apache Thrift (Go)
workload: Echo RPC, Protobuf payload 581 bytes, client and server on the same machine, 500/2000/5000 concurrent clients, 0ms/10ms/30ms simulated processing time.
claimed_speedup: ~1.5x higher throughput than grpc-go (e.g. ~200,000 vs ~130,000 calls/s at 2000-5000 concurrent clients, 0ms processing) and roughly 3x higher than Apache Thrift-Go (~200,000 vs ~55,000-70,000 calls/s) (derived from page data: p0-throughput.png chart, values read off the chart, approximate)
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU E5-2630 v3 @ 2.40GHz, 32 cores, 32GB RAM, CentOS 7 / kernel 3.10.0-229.el7.x86_64
tradeoffs: Uses its own service-discovery/governance stack (zookeeper/etcd/consul) layered on top of the RPC core; multiple codecs supported (Protobuf/JSON/MessagePack) with the compared numbers specific to Protobuf.
caveats: Benchmark dates to a 2018 blog post (colobu.com) and used Go 1.9.0; grpc-go and Thrift-Go have both changed substantially since, so the current gap is unverified and likely different. Numbers were read off a chart image rather than a raw data table. GitHub's license API misreports this repo as 'Other/NOASSERTION'; the actual LICENSE file text is Apache License 2.0 (recorded here from the file content).
found_via: gh api repos/smallnest/rpcx/readme (Performance section) -> linked rpcx-benchmark repo and colobu.com 2018 chart

name: sockudo-ws
workload: Plaintext WebSocket echo server, payload sizes 512 and 1024 bytes, 100 and 500 concurrent connections, messages/sec (using the denoland/fastwebsockets benches harness).
claimed_speedup: 1.02x-1.03x higher msg/s than uWebSockets v20.64 across the 4 tested cases (e.g. 232,712 vs 227,973 msg/s at 512B/100 conns; 232,072 vs 224,498 msg/s at 1024B/100 conns; 231,135 vs 222,493 msg/s at 512B/500 conns; 222,578 vs 216,833 msg/s at 1024B/500 conns)
tradeoffs: Rust safety/ergonomics vs uWebSockets' raw C++ API; sockudo-ws is a newer, much less battle-tested library than uWebSockets, which underpins many production Node.js/Bun stacks.
caveats: Margin over uWebSockets is small (2-3%), which is within plausible run-to-run noise for a single-machine microbenchmark; numbers are self-reported by the sockudo-ws project rather than independently reproduced, though the benchmark harness itself (denoland/fastwebsockets benches) is a neutral third-party suite and reproduction steps are given.
found_via: Hacker News (hn.algolia.com) search 'WebSocket server benchmark' -> Show HN: Sockudo -> sockudo/sockudo-ws README Performance section
